item.title: Obama to Headline Democratic Redistricting Fund-Raiser
item.description:
Former President Barack Obama will hold a fund-raiser in late August for the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, a fresh sign that Democrats intend to continue their aggressive push to gerrymander congressional districts ahead of the 2028 election.

The fund-raiser will take place on Martha’s Vineyard and will be hosted by Eric Holder, the former attorney general under Mr. Obama and the chairman of the committee, which is the main Democratic group focused on redistricting.

While Democrats appear to have exhausted all of their options for new maps before the midterm elections this year, their focus on the 2028 election still requires investment in crucial, state-level elections this fall. Democrats hope to protect or build trifectas in various states — single-party control of both chambers of legislatures plus the governor’s office — or Democratic supermajorities that would allow them to override a hostile governor’s veto.

The emergence of Mr. Obama on the political fund-raising circuit comes as Democrats, at least at the national level, are facing a significant cash shortfall.

Drawing even with Republicans in the national redistricting wars has been a top priority for Mr. Holder, Mr. Obama and Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic House minority leader. Mr. Obama, who remains one of the party’s most popular and influential figures, was a prominent supporter of a congressional gerrymander in California and an attempted one in Virginia.

“The race by Republicans to gerrymander is not over — and between potential redraws and the November election, the 2028 redistricting fight is already underway,” John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, said in a statement on Tuesday.

Details of the fund-raiser were first reported by Punchbowl News.

Democrats have largely been playing catch-up on the national redistricting front. Ever since President Trump sparked the battle by imploring Republicans in Texas to take the rare partisan step of redrawing their congressional map last year to benefit Republicans in the midterms, Democrats have faced a host of hurdles, largely because of redistricting reforms pushed by Mr. Obama, Mr. Holder and other Democrats.

The result has been the creation of as many as a dozen new districts that will favor Republicans this year.

Democrats have turned their attention to 2028 with the goal of reversing that new advantage and then some. States including New York, Virginia, Illinois and Maryland have all signaled a desire to redraw their maps for the next cycle. California could also try to redraw its map yet again, and some Democrats hope Washington and Oregon will join the battle, as well.

Republicans are also poised to redraw maps in many states in 2028, including Indiana, Mississippi, Nebraska and Kansas — as well as states redrawn in the past year, including Texas, Alabama and Louisiana, where further opportunities may lie.

item.title: Graham and Netanyahu Worked Together to Denounce International Criminal Court
item.description:
Senator Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina Republican who died this month at 71, worked privately with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel to coordinate a bipartisan group of lawmakers to denounce the International Criminal Court investigation into Mr. Netanyahu just before the 2024 election, footage of their discussions shows.

The conversations were among roughly 400 hours recorded by the British filmmaker Alex Holder, who trailed Mr. Graham for roughly four years for a planned documentary project titled “Lindsey’s Game.” The footage of two discussions with Mr. Netanyahu about rebuking the I.C.C. was reviewed by The New York Times.

The calls took place just days before the 2024 election, on Oct. 29, as Mr. Graham was in Ohio, where he was campaigning with Donald Trump Jr. for Bernie Moreno in a Senate race, according to Mr. Holder.

The discussions underscore the significance of the relationship between Mr. Graham and Mr. Netanyahu and its impact, including with the senator’s colleagues. The two men were days away from an election that would return Donald J. Trump to the White House. Mr. Graham was a valuable interlocutor for Mr. Netanyahu even before that, but the call took place as the prime minister was prepared to discuss with Mr. Trump waging an increasingly expansive war against Iran.

Mr. Netanyahu was in Washington on Tuesday for Mr. Graham’s funeral, as well as a meeting with Mr. Trump about the war in Iran, which is becoming an intractable problem for the president.

Mr. Netanyahu remains the subject of an arrest warrant by the I.C.C., but Israeli officials have called the effort politically motivated. Mr. Netanyahu has made foreign trips since it was issued, and is set to travel to the U.N. General Assembly in New York in September.

Mr. Trump has declared that he will not be arrested, despite Mayor Zohran Mamdani calling Mr. Netanyahu a war criminal and saying he had reviewed whether city officials had the power to make an arrest. The mayor later said officials concluded they did not.

In the first call with Mr. Netanyahu, which was recorded on video, Mr. Graham is seen and heard talking to the prime minister, whose voice is occasionally garbled as it comes through the line and is picked up on the senator’s microphone. But Mr. Netanyahu could be heard clearly as he discussed a pending decision by the I.C.C. about whether to seek his arrest for alleged war crimes, as a prosecutor with the court had recommended earlier in 2024.

“A three-judge panel,” Mr. Netanyahu said in the first call with Mr. Graham, will be “making the decision very soon.” He noted that the court’s chief prosecutor, Karim A. A. Khan, had faced allegations of sexual misconduct, and suggested to Mr. Graham that “the great cloud that it shed” could help delay the arrest warrant (Mr. Khan was removed from his position last week, the court’s oversight body announced.)

“It is possible to have to appeal to the court to say, ‘OK, we want to review this before you do anything, before you issue an arrest warrant. There has to be a review about this entire process,’” Mr. Netanyahu said, adding that “this cloud or this stain has to be removed” before moving forward.

“And I suggest that you send a letter, with, maybe some other senators,”Mr. Netanyahu said. When Mr. Graham offered up Speaker Mike Johnson as the “perfect person” to sign such a letter, Mr. Netanyahu replied, “Would he get Democrats?”

Mr. Graham said that he would try for a bipartisan approach.

Mr. Holder recorded the audio, without video, of a second call between the two men that he said took place later that day. Only Mr. Graham’s voice could be heard.

On that call, Mr. Graham joked to Mr. Netanyahu that he should “pay me for all this. I should get tons of shekels.” It would take “more than dinner,” he added.

He then said that “we got them both,” appearing to refer to Senators Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Ben Cardin of Maryland, two Democrats, who said they would sign a letter protesting the efforts to move ahead with an arrest warrant.

“So here’s why I’m calling you,” Mr. Graham told Mr. Netanyahu, saying he hoped to get the letter “out the door Wednesday,” appearing to refer to the next day, October 30. “So send me over whatever you want to say. And they want to say two things” to the I.C.C.

One was that the prosecutors should speak with the Israeli government and not move ahead with the case until “the cloud is lifted” from the prosecutor’s own problems.

What Mr. Graham requested in exchange, he said, was for Mr. Netanyahu “to call Blumenthal and Cardin and thank them for being fair-minded on this, and also thank them for trying to help with Saudi-Israel normalization. You appreciate it. You’re very interested in it, and that will encourage both of them.”

The letter was released on Nov. 1, 2024, and included Mr. Blumenthal and Mr. Cardin as signers. In addition to noting the allegations against Mr. Khan, the letter said that the I.C.C. did “not comply” with the law by declining to keep a planned meeting with Israeli representatives before applying for the arrest warrant.

A spokesman for Mr. Netanyahu did not respond to an email seeking comment on the calls.

Mr. Blumenthal declined to address questions about the calls Mr. Graham had with Mr. Netanyahu. An aide to Mr. Cardin did not respond to an email seeking comment.

item.title: Trump’s Spy Chief Spends Final Hours in Job Boasting of Mass Firings
item.description:
Bill Pulte, the acting director of national intelligence, has spent his final days on the job celebrating his efforts to terminate employees in his office.

But current and former officials said few people have actually been fired in recent weeks from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, despite a flurry of social media posts by Mr. Pulte. And members of Congress have been left scratching their heads about whether Mr. Pulte has cut nearly as many employees as he has claimed.

Mr. Pulte said on Tuesday, hours before the Senate is expected to confirm his replacement, Jay Clayton, that he had reduced the staff at his organization by nearly a third since taking the job of spy chief in June.

“Good News! In addition to the Historic DECLASSIFICATIONS (Transparency!) by the President, we are, this morning, Executing a 5th and Near Final Round of TERMINATIONS, an approximately 30% Staff Reduction from Weeks Ago,” Mr. Pulte wrote in an X post that mimicked President Trump’s social media patois. “The Intelligence Community must protect the American people, NOT the political whims of the bloated and corrupt elite class.”

But Mr. Pulte’s office has provided no details or explanations of the purported cuts, sowing doubts on Capitol Hill.

Mr. Pulte, who also oversees a federal housing agency and has pursued campaigns of retribution against Mr. Trump’s perceived enemies, lacked any national security experience before he was tapped to run the spy office.

“The acting D.N.I. has been quick to announce firings and make public claims about them, but has so far declined to provide the Senate Intelligence Committee with the information necessary to assess the accuracy of those statements or the basis for those decisions,” said Rachel Cohen, a spokeswoman for Senator Mark Warner of Virginia, the top Democrat on the committee.

Mr. Pulte has not laid out the goals of his purported reductions. A spokeswoman for Mr. Pulte did not respond to questions about his social media posts.

But several former U.S. intelligence officials expressed disbelief about the claim of reductions. They said Mr. Pulte was counting people whose tour of duty at the office was complete and were returning to their home agencies as previously planned. He also appears to be counting unfilled positions at the National Counterterrorism Center and other parts of the spy office as terminations, former officials said.

Still, current and former officials said, the elimination of jobs and returning officers to their home agencies have hit hardest at the National Intelligence Council, a group that reviews the conclusions of a variety of spy agencies.

In many respects, the council is a core part of the spy chief’s office, developing authoritative analytic judgments supported by a variety of intelligence agencies, while guarding against groupthink.

Last year, Tulsi Gabbard, the previous director, fired the head of the council in a dispute over intelligence about a Venezuelan gang. She also eliminated the council’s Strategic Futures Group, arguing its work was at odds with Mr. Trump’s policies.

The Office of the Director of National Intelligence had about 1,700 employees when Ms. Gabbard announced in May that she was stepping down, including around 1,300 full-time government employees and 400 contractors.

Mr. Pulte initially put a handful of close aides to Ms. Gabbard on administrative leave, allowing them to find other jobs in the government. He also directed about 75 intelligence officers who formally worked for other spy agencies, like the C.I.A., the National Security Agency, the Defense Intelligence Agency or others, to return to those agencies.

Julia Curlee, a former longtime C.I.A. analyst who left the agency this year, criticized Mr. Pulte’s efforts to cut intelligence professionals as a performance intended to please Mr. Trump that may have long-term consequences for America’s spy agencies.

“The bill will come due in low morale and in Americans who now won’t apply,” said Ms. Curlee, who served on the White House National Security Council during the first few months of the second Trump administration. “Congress should demand to know what this is meant to achieve, and which national security functions will go unperformed.”

item.title: Senators Forge a Deal on Graham’s Russia Sanctions Bill
item.description:
Senators on Tuesday announced a breakthrough in a long-stalled bipartisan effort to advance sweeping sanctions against Russia, paving the way for an evening test vote on the compromise bill after the Washington funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, its main champion.

Republicans and Democrats said they had addressed concerns from members of both parties and were ready to push ahead in efforts to pass the measure in honor of Mr. Graham, who spent the final hours of his life working in Ukraine to cement it.

The measure would impose harsh new penalties on countries that purchase oil and other energy products from Russia, as well as extend existing sanctions against Iran seeking to limit its ability to fuel its wartime economy.

“We are proud to announce an agreement on legislation to stop purchasers of Russian oil and gas from fueling Putin’s war machine and to continue restricting the Iranian regime’s ability to support terrorism and build its nuclear program,” said a joint statement from the Republican senators Darline Graham of South Carolina, Jim Risch of Idaho, Roger Wicker of Mississippi and Katie Britt of Alabama and the Democratic senators Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire. “There is no greater way to honor Senator Graham’s legacy than to move forward with this bipartisan agreement, and we look forward to today’s vote.”

The announcement came just as lawmakers and his family gathered at the Capitol to honor Mr. Graham’s life, and hours before the president and world leaders convened at the National Cathedral for his funeral.

An initial vote was expected on Tuesday evening, just after President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, who has long pressed for such a sanctions package, was to meet with senators on Capitol Hill.

The revised legislation reflects an intense round of negotiations to narrow the measure’s provisions and ensure tighter congressional oversight over the penalties it would impose.

To appease Democrats who had balked at handing President Trump new tariff authority, the revised measure would require that the president impose the sanctions rather than simply permit him to do so — though Mr. Trump could still waive them if he certified that it was necessary for national security reasons. Negotiators also added requirements that the administration regularly report to Congress on how the penalties were being carried out.

Senators also said they had adjusted language governing the bill’s secondary tariffs to exempt American allies that still purchase small amounts of oil, gas and other energy from Russia if they were demonstrably reducing their reliance on Russian-produced energy.

Mr. Blumenthal, who had worked with Mr. Graham on the measure for more than a year, said he was confident the changes would secure enough backing to overcome any objections from Democrats and yield the votes necessary for the measure to move ahead.

“We’ve got a solid core of 60-plus senators,” Mr. Blumenthal said.

item.title: Who Wins (and Who Loses) in the Democrats’ New 2028 Primary Calendar?
item.description:
Democrats across the country agree that their new primary map will redraw the road to their party’s 2028 presidential nomination. But, as they look to what’s widely expected to be a crowded and competitive contest, no one is quite sure what turns it will take.

Instead of Iowa and New Hampshire, long the traditional openers of the primary process, Democratic candidates will navigate their way through a six-state gantlet that starts in South Carolina on Jan. 22, winds through Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico and Michigan and ends in Virginia on Feb. 29.

The cross-country sprint has significantly broadened the race — geographically, racially and ideologically, Democratic strategists say.

“It really could benefit anyone,” said Rob Flaherty, a deputy campaign manager for former Vice President Kamala Harris’s 2024 run and the co-host of “Nobody Knows Anything,” a podcast about national politics. “I follow things pretty closely, and I have no idea how it’s going to bounce.”

Here’s what the calendar does — and doesn’t — tell us about the 2028 Democratic primary race.

The new map is good news for Black voters, increasing their power in the earliest stage of the contest. While the electorate in Iowa and New Hampshire is largely white, a majority of South Carolina Democratic primary voters are Black.

“Black voters are the backbone of this party,” said Christale Spain, the chair of the state’s Democratic Party, in an interview with the political commentator Roland Martin last week. “We should continue to elevate Black voters role in the process.”

Harris, who has floated the possibility of a third presidential run, remains popular with Black voters and could be advantaged by South Carolina’s spot at the head of the line — but it’s hard to predict. In 2020, she exited the race before the state even voted, with her fund-raising having run dry.

Some commentators pointed to the possibility that multiple Black candidates — including perhaps Gov. Wes Moore of Maryland and Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia — could split the electorate, sending the race into the next contests with muddled results.

Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, who has a history of building coalitions with Black voters, could be strong in the state. Pete Buttigieg, the former transportation secretary, struggled there in 2020.

The new map more than doubles the share of Latino voters across the first four states from 2020, the last time Democrats had a competitive presidential primary, according to an analysis by Decision Desk HQ, an election results reporting website.

The heavy Latino populations in Nevada and New Mexico give those voters a pivotal role in culling the field as the candidates move through the early contests.

While Latino voters are generally considered more socially moderate, Senator Bernie Sanders, the liberal Vermont independent, won big in Nevada after investing heavily in organizing there in 2020. Working-class Latino voters could also be inclined toward candidates like Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York or Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona.

“The Black voters are going to kick off the calendar,” said Xochitl Hinojosa, a Democratic strategist. “But I do think that Latino voters will ultimately decide who the nominee is.”

The announcement of the new calendar prompted grumbles from some corners of the progressive world that the Democratic National Committee had created a schedule designed to hamper insurgent left-wing candidates.

But it’s not clear what kind of candidate is favored by the new calendar.

The six early states are relatively inexpensive to advertise in, which could provide the opportunity for an insurgent to catch fire — though in 2020, South Carolina elevated Joseph R. Biden Jr., an establishment candidate, over Mr. Sanders.

On the other hand, the new map rewards campaigns with the money to build a six-state, cross-country organization that can reach diverse constituencies. That may benefit candidates like Ms. Harris and Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, who could enter the race with well-established political brands and expansive fund-raising lists.

One of the biggest changes to the calendar is bumping New Hampshire from its vaunted “first in the nation” position.

New Hampshire law requires the state’s presidential primary to be held at least seven days before any “similar election.” That standard would bump its primary into mid-January, before South Carolina.

In past elections, New Hampshire has been immovable. In 2024, party leaders also tried to move the state back in the calendar. It voted first anyhow, risking its delegates in the process.

Local officials have promised to once again defend the state’s tradition. But in 2028, the penalties for candidates could be onerous: The party has threatened to bar any candidate who campaigns in a state that jumps the calendar from participating in official party debates.

That change could hurt Mr. Buttigieg, who has shown strength in the state.

New Hampshire also runs an open primary, allowing independent voters to participate in party contests. That dynamic has made it a place where moderates can gain steam — a benefit such candidates will no longer get.

item.title: Behind Closed Doors, Trump Huddles With Netanyahu and Zelensky
item.description:
One of the most predictable things about this unpredictable president is how much he enjoys bringing world leaders into the Oval Office, a global symbol of American power. The only thing President Trump seems to enjoy more than showing off his gilded room is letting a wall of news photographers and reporters capture him as he does it.

So it was revealing that Mr. Trump kept two Tuesday audiences — one with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, and the other with President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine — out of the public eye. It was also unusual that Mr. Trump then spent the day letting his two visitors sum up the meetings.

Mr. Netanyahu and Mr. Zelensky both need the symbolism of an Oval Office visit to convey solidarity with Mr. Trump and bolster domestic support for their respective military campaigns. But over time, they have become symbols, too: of intractable conflicts with U.S. adversaries, and of Mr. Trump’s failed promises to end them.

“I have just finished an excellent meeting with President Trump,” Mr. Netanyahu said in a statement. “When I say excellent, it’s not just lip service. It was a conversation of full partnership, of mutual support, with an understanding of the shared goal to ensure that Iran will not have nuclear weapons, and also other goals.”

He added: “It was one of the best conversations I’ve had with the president of the United States, our friend Donald Trump.”

In his own statement, Mr. Zelensky said that his hourlong meeting with Mr. Trump, held just before Mr. Netanyahu’s, was about restarting stalled diplomatic efforts to end a more than four-year-long war with Russia. Mr. Trump also appeared to be keeping to an earlier commitment to allow Ukraine to manufacture the Patriot air defense interceptors that Mr. Zelensky’s military needs to defend against Russian ballistic missile attacks. But those weapons systems could take months or years to manufacture, so the Ukrainian president has long pushed for more U.S. help with weapons, a request he hinted at in his statement.

“The president and I discussed licenses for Patriot interceptor production and several other ideas that could help,” Mr. Zelensky said. “We also spoke about diplomacy — it’s important that the diplomatic process be reinvigorated.”

Mr. Netanyahu and Mr. Zelensky are facing their own challenges domestically, and their appearances in Washington underscored just how deeply Mr. Trump’s own political fortunes had become enmeshed with theirs.

A Ukrainian strike last weekend on an Iranian cargo ship in the Caspian Sea has caused fresh concerns that the two wars are melding into a slow-boil global conflict. Russia has hit Ukraine with Iranian drones. Ukraine is now exporting its low-cost anti-drone systems to Gulf Countries. In the middle of it all is Mr. Trump, whose decision to join Mr. Netanyahu at war with Iran has left him unable to bring a patient adversary to the negotiating table.

“He clearly has worsened his party’s prospects for the midterms,” said John E. Herbst, a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine who is now the senior director of the Atlantic Council’s Eurasia Center. “Trump does not like being bullied, but he is being bullied, and there’s only so much he can do about it.”

Mr. Netanyahu’s trip to the United States was the seventh he had made in Mr. Trump’s second term. In one fateful February meeting, Mr. Netanyahu laid the groundwork to convince Mr. Trump that Tehran was ripe for regime change, and expressed his belief that a joint U.S.-Israeli mission could accomplish it.

Five months later, the Iranians have endured the killing of the country’s supreme leader, and regular airstrikes by U.S. forces. The economically crucial Strait of Hormuz remains controlled by the powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, who are in no rush to acquiesce to the president’s demands to open it.

The fighting has paused, in part because Mr. Trump's advisers have grown increasingly concerned about the Pentagon’s already diminished stockpile of Patriot antimissile interceptors and other air defense munitions in the Middle East.

The war is also deeply unpopular, and Americans have signaled that they do not understand what the United States is doing in Iran. One in three Americans support the war, according to a poll released this week by Reuters/Ipsos. A CBS News/YouGov poll released this week showed that 76 percent of Americans believe the war has become much harder than the president expected. According to that poll, two-thirds of Americans believe the United States should end the war.

In an interview on Tuesday morning with “Fox & Friends,” Mr. Trump downplayed reports that Mr. Netanyahu would present new information about an uptick in activity at Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected Iranian nuclear site. And he betrayed some annoyance with his guest.

“I don’t need Bibi to tell me that,” Mr. Trump said. “Bibi is telling me that because he wants me to stay involved.” He added, “We took out their nuclear sites, and we’ll have to take out Pickaxe if we don’t make a deal.”

On Tuesday, Mr. Netanyahu slipped into the White House through a side door. In the Oval Office, he was joined by the Israeli ambassador, Yechiel Leiter, and his national security adviser, Shmuel Ben Ezra.

For his part, Mr. Zelensky, once mocked by a conservative reporter in the Oval Office for turning up at the White House in military-style fatigues, donned a black suit jacket. In the past, Mr. Trump has seemed to relish pushing Mr. Zelensky around, particularly in an Oval Office meeting early last year that went so poorly that the president told the Ukrainian leader to leave. But as the war has dragged on, Mr. Zelensky has shown resilience and momentum, and Mr. Trump likes winners.

“President Putin will be waiting to see how long that lasts,” Evelyn Farkas, the executive director of the McCain Institute, said of the Russian leader. Ms. Farkas, a former Obama administration deputy assistant secretary of defense who handled Russian policy, added: “Because President Trump isn’t known for his consistency when it comes to these kinds of negotiations.”

The White House kept news of the meetings brief: “Both meetings were positive and productive!” Karoline Leavitt, the press secretary, wrote on X. Mr. Trump was focused on other matters, including traveling to the National Cathedral to deliver a memorial speech for Senator Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina Republican who died earlier this month.

“He never saw a war that he didn’t like,” the president said of the senator.

Mr. Netanyahu and Mr. Zelensky both sat nearby, listening intently.

Johnatan Reiss contributed reporting from Tel Aviv, and Isabel Kershner from Jerusalem.

item.title: Iran Considered Retaliatory Strike on Ukrainian Seaport
item.description:
Iran considered attacking a seaport in Ukraine in response to a Ukrainian strike on an Iranian ship, but a flurry of diplomacy has calmed the situation for now, according to Iranian and Western officials.

Ukraine, which has accused Iran and Russia of supporting each other’s military operations, struck an Iranian commercial cargo ship in the Caspian Sea on Saturday, killing a civilian sailor. Iranian officials vowed to retaliate.

Some people briefed on the intelligence said that they expected Iran to fire a ballistic missile with a small warhead at Ukraine, to make a symbolic point but cause relatively little damage. Other officials said the target was probably one of Ukraine’s Black Sea ports.

Any missile fired from Iran into Ukraine would be a dramatic escalation and risk triggering a wider war, given the tensions between the two countries over Iran’s alliance with Russia.

Iranian officials said they hoped the conflict would end with their retaliatory strike, but Western officials warned that it was difficult to predict how Ukraine would respond.

The officials interviewed for this article spoke on the condition of anonymity — the Western officials so they could discuss sensitive intelligence matters, and the Iranians so they could discuss military planning.

On Sunday, Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign minister, called Ukraine’s attack a violation of the U.N. charter aimed at dragging Europe into Iran’s war with the United States. In a social media post, he said the incident “CANNOT GO UNANSWERED.”

A U.S. blockade of Iranian Persian Gulf ports has made Iran’s trade with Russia across the Caspian Sea more important. The Caspian Sea has emerged as a critical supply route for both overt and covert trade.

But on Tuesday, after Ukrainian diplomats sought to ease tensions, Mr. Araghchi spoke by phone with his Ukrainian counterpart, Andrii Sybiha.

After the call, Mr. Araghchi said in a post that Mr. Sybiha had described the attack on the cargo ship as unintentional. “Iran does not seek escalation either, but made clear any attack on our citizens or interests is unacceptable,” Mr. Araghchi wrote. “There must be restitution for losses.”

The Iranian foreign minister said on his official webpage that he also spoke to Kaja Kallas, the top European Union diplomat, about “ways to help decrease tensions in the region.”

Mehdi Rahmati, an analyst who is close to Iran’s government and is based in the country, said that while some Iranian political figures had called for striking back at Ukraine, others had advised restraint.

“Ukraine is not a small, insignificant country. It has warfare experience, and logistical support from America and Europe. We won’t gain anything by creating a new front in the war,” Mr. Rahmati said in a phone interview from Tehran.

Still, it was not clear how long the tensions would remain in check.

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine was in Washington on Tuesday for a meeting with President Trump and a memorial service for Senator Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina Republican who supported Ukraine in its war against Russia.

Mr. Zelensky had promised to bring intelligence about Russia’s support for Iran in its war with the United States. Ukrainian officials have said that Russia has given Iran satellite imagery of U.S. bases in the Middle East.

Ukrainian officials have long complained about Russia’s use of Iranian drones and drone parts in its attacks on Ukraine.

item.title: Trump Asks Supreme Court to Overturn $83.3 Million Award in Carroll Defamation Case
item.description:
President Trump on Tuesday asked the Supreme Court to step in and overturn an $83.3 million jury award against him for defaming the writer E. Jean Carroll after she accused him of a decades-old sexual assault in a Manhattan department store.

The president urged the justices to reject the jury’s award, asserting that the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision granting presidents sweeping immunity for actions they take in office shielded him from liability in the case.

“This is the first case in our nation’s history in which a court has imposed damages liability on a president for his conduct in office,” Mr. Trump’s lawyers said in a filing to the court reviewed The New York Times.

Lawyers for Mr. Trump asserted that the question of whether he had immunity in the case was “straightforward on the undisputed factual record.” An appeals court had rejected that argument. Mr. Trump’s lawyers told the court that if the ruling was allowed to stand, it would cause “significant damage,” harming not only Mr. Trump but also future presidents and the nation.

The petition to the justices is the latest turn in Mr. Trump’s continued efforts to deny Ms. Carroll’s claims and avoid two separate monetary awards that juries ordered him to pay related to Ms. Carroll’s allegations that Mr. Trump sexually assaulted her in a Bergdorf Goodman dressing room in the mid-1990s and then defamed her in a series of statements and social media posts.

Lawyers for the Justice Department separately also asked the justices to take up the case, according to a filing to the court reviewed by The Times.

Ms. Carroll’s legal team declined a request for comment.

In late June, the Supreme Court rejected a separate request from Mr. Trump that the court review a $5 million judgment against him from a previous 2023 jury finding that he had sexually abused and defamed Ms. Carroll.

The court’s decision not to hear that case prompted a trial court judge to order that the money, which had been held in escrow while Mr. Trump appealed, be paid to Ms. Carroll.

Mr. Trump’s new petition relates to a far larger judgment awarded by a Manhattan jury in 2024. That jury awarded Ms. Carroll $65 million in punitive damages after determining that Mr. Trump had acted with malice in verbally attacking her in social media posts, at news conferences and during the trial. The jury also awarded Ms. Carroll $18.3 million in compensatory damages for her suffering.

At the time, Mr. Trump called the verdict “absolutely ridiculous” on social media.

“Our Legal System is out of control, and being used as a Political Weapon,” he added, and pledged to appeal. “They have taken away all First Amendment Rights.”

Got a news tip about the courts? If you have information to share about the Supreme Court or other federal courts, please contact us.

The Supreme Court is currently on its summer recess, and the justices are not likely to consider whether to take up the case until late September, when they meet for their annual “long conference,” at which they consider thousands of pending petitions — and reject most of them.

Mr. Trump has pursued various efforts to overturn the verdict, so far unsuccessfully.

In September, a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit unanimously upheld the jury’s 2024 award. The panel rejected arguments by Mr. Trump’s legal team that he was insulated from liability because of the Supreme Court’s presidential immunity decision.

In a decision that greatly expanded presidential power, the justices — split along partisan lines — found that Mr. Trump was entitled to substantial immunity from criminal prosecution on charges that he tried to overturn the 2020 election. The court’s conservative majority agreed that presidents can be shielded from actions taken in office as part of their official duties that could later be used against them by political opponents.

Lawyers for Mr. Trump have argued that his statements about Ms. Carroll, which came during his first term as president, were “official presidential statements” and thus could not be used as evidence against him to impose liability.

In its ruling, the appeals court judges rejected that position, writing that Mr. Trump “never wavered or relented in his public attacks” against Ms. Carroll, who is 82. The panel also said that he had assailed her “as a politically and financially motivated liar, insinuating that she was too unattractive for him to have sexually assaulted her and threatening that she would ‘pay dearly’ for speaking out.”

Mr. Trump’s lawyers then asked the full appeals court to hear the case, which is called en banc review. In late April, a divided appeals court declined to take up the case.

In its petition to the justices, Mr. Trump’s legal team, citing to the 2024 Supreme Court immunity case, asserted that the appeals court had “refused to apply presidential immunity even after this court recognized that ‘most of a president’s public communications are likely to fall comfortably within’ that protection.”

Though Ms. Carroll has already been paid the judgment from the 2023 case, the president is nevertheless asking the Supreme Court to revisit its June decision not to intervene in that matter, too. Lawyers for the president have said the justices should hear challenges to both verdicts together.

Supreme Court rules provide parties a pathway to request a rehearing once the court has denied a petition. It is rare but not unprecedented for the justices to grant such requests.

The justices did not provide any reasoning for their decision to reject the case, which is typical when the court declines to hear petitions.

After the justices rejected the case, Mr. Trump called Ms. Carroll’s lawsuit “a Fake Case,” writing on social media that he would “continue the fight against this Weaponization and Lawfare Case against me, including the ridiculous claim of Defamation, with all of my power and strength.”

item.title: A U.S. Citizen Deleted His Phone’s Data. Now He Faces a Felony Charge.
item.description:
It sounds like something that James Bond would use: a gadget that self-destructs if it falls into the wrong hands. But it’s actually an open-source operating system that can be downloaded onto Android phones.

Federal prosecutors in Atlanta are bringing an obstruction charge against a U.S. citizen who gave customs officers what is known as a duress passcode, which activated software that erased the contents of his phone.

The authorities stopped Samuel Tunick, an Atlanta resident, for interrogation at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport as he returned to the United States on Jan. 24 last year, according to a November grand jury indictment. The authorities seized his phone before allowing him to enter the country. A hearing on the case was held last week in federal court in Atlanta.

The prosecution is one of the earliest known instances of federal authorities charging a person with destroying evidence with a program designed to wipe a device when a specific code is entered.

Mr. Tunick’s lawyers argued during the hearing last week that the seizure was unlawful, and that he was targeted because of his political activism against Atlanta’s plan to build a police and fire training center within a 1,000-acre stretch of urban woodland. Opponents argue that the center, known as Cop City, would militarize officers and destroy precious green space.

The federal statute underlying the charge makes it a felony to destroy evidence or transfer assets to keep the government from seizing them, or to tip someone off about an upcoming search or wiretap. It carries a penalty of up to five years in federal prison, a fine, or both.

The act applies before, during or after a search. If the target of an investigation knows that a search or seizure is imminent, and that person acts to thwart it, they would fall under the statute, experts said.

Courts have long treated digital data as property — think about intellectual property theft as one example — so a software wipe is treated in the legal system no differently than flushing physical evidence.

The government’s argument here is that the physical phone was just a container. The data itself was the property that they had lawful authority to seize, and inputting the duress code was the physical act that caused its destruction.

“The statute says explicitly it has to be for the purpose of preventing or impairing the government’s lawful authority,” said Daniel Richman, a law professor at Columbia University and a former prosecutor in the U.S. Attorney’s Office. “The key is he gave the code to the government, knowing that the entry of this code would erase the evidence.”

That it was a border search is central to both the government’s prosecution and the defense’s legal challenge.

Customs and border authorities believe that they have the right to search and seize incoming travelers’ digital devices without a search warrant or court order because travelers are not on U.S. soil until they’re authorized to enter.

Mr. Tunick, who was returning from a vacation in the Dominican Republic, and his lawyers argue that even at an international airport, travelers retain vital protections. They said that he was subjected to an unlawful detention, was never read his rights and was repeatedly denied requests to speak with a lawyer.

His lawyers were not immediately available for comment on Tuesday.

A duress passcode is a privacy and security feature in which a user has previously configured a secondary passcode that is not their usual code to unlock the screen. If the user is forced or pressured to hand over their phone, they can provide this passcode instead of the one that unlocks their phone.

When the duress passcode is entered, rather than unlocking the phone, the operating system starts a full wipe of the device’s digital contents. The process leaves the physical device and hardware intact while completely erasing the underlying digital data.

In Mr. Tunick’s case, he used GrapheneOS, a private mobile operating system compatible with some Android phones.

“Many times the government wants to highlight what it was trying to investigate because that ups the stakes on what the defendant was doing,” Professor Richman said. “This is a case where I think they’re trying to avoid exactly that by focusing only on the destruction, and not what the investigation was about.”

The statute that is being used in this case has seldom been cited. It does not require the government to prove or explain the underlying investigation. A statute that is typically used carries a heavier maximum penalty of 20 years, but its use often forces the government to detail their underlying investigation.

“Whether they’ll succeed or not remains to be seen, if this goes to trial,” he said.

Professor Richman suggested that if a traveler decided to delete everything on their phone before going through an airport checkpoint simply because they did not want the government looking at their personal files, they have a strong argument that they did not act with the specific criminal intent to thwart an imminent search.

But there’s a turning point once you are stopped and actively being questioned.

“Intentionally giving a wipe code to people you know to be exercising lawful authority,” he said, “is going to put you squarely in the realm of the statute.”

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: What’s Going on With Mitch McConnell? Kentucky’s Governor Has Questions.
item.description:
Are you there, Senator McConnell? It’s me, Governor Beshear.

More than six weeks after Senator Mitch McConnell, the former Republican leader from Kentucky, entered the hospital and vanished from public life, the state’s ambitious Democratic governor, Andy Beshear, sent him a letter.

“I am addressing this letter to Senator McConnell under the assumption that he is capable of reading and responding verbally, and not incapacitated by means of consciousness or cognition,” the governor began. He went on to call on Mr. McConnell to “directly and verbally address the people of Kentucky and provide proof of your capacity to serve, or resign.”

With his request for proof of life, Mr. Beshear, 48, was seizing on — and stoking — the frenzied speculation that has swirled on both the left and the far right ever since Mr. McConnell, 84, was hospitalized in mid-June.

And it was an unusual attempt by a politician to puncture the veil of decorum that has long been afforded to aging politicians in the Senate, where more than a third of the senators are now 70 or older.

“If you are unwilling to voluntarily show that you still have the capacity to serve,” Mr. Beshear wrote, he would “insist” that Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota and the majority leader, investigate Mr. McConnell’s condition.

Mr. Thune told NBC News Tuesday that he had not seen the letter, but he dismissed the possibility of getting involved. “I think that’s an issue, really, that’s between Senator McConnell and the people of Kentucky,” he said. He spoke after attending a memorial service for Senator Lindsey Graham, who died this month at the age of 71.

A spokesman for Mr. McConnell, who is planning to retire in January, did not respond to a request for comment.

Calls for new leadership in both political parties have intensified the public’s focus on an aging Washington.

It’s a potent political issue, but it can be a tricky one to press, since age and illness are nonpartisan. President Trump, who turned 80 this year, is facing new scrutiny over his health; Democrats are still reckoning with their support of former President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s doomed re-election bid at the age of 81.

(Mr. Beshear was among the Democrats who had said he would support Mr. Biden’s campaign in the days after a disastrous debate performance renewed questions about his fitness for office.)

Mr. McConnell, who was once an outsize presence in American politics, has been all but invisible since he was admitted to the hospital on June 14.

Emergency operators had been heard that morning saying they were performing CPR on an unconscious individual suffering cardiac arrest at Mr. McConnell’s address in Washington; his office initially refused to comment on those recordings. The silence fueled speculation and demands for transparency, including from right-wing figures like Laura Loomer and Glenn Beck.

On July 12, Mr. McConnell’s aides released a written statement from the senator, in which he said he had suffered a fall that left him briefly unconscious. “I didn’t have a heart attack or a stroke,” it said. “I don’t have any tumors or hemorrhages.”

People in Washington and beyond parsed the accompanying photograph, which showed Mr. McConnell and his wife, Elaine Chao — along with the front page of that day’s Washington Post’s Sports section.

Mr. Beshear has taken an intense public interest in Mr. McConnell’s health in recent weeks, urging Mr. McConnell to provide more information. He has also fed the rumor mill himself.

“I’ve gotten two calls from different agencies, not state agencies, suggesting he’d passed,” Mr. Beshear said, without elaborating, in an interview earlier this month with Katie Couric on YouTube, adding that he thought Mr. McConnell’s reticence had fueled speculation.

This week, Mr. McConnell’s office released another statement in which the senator said he would not be returning to Washington this week, and that he would miss Saturday’s Fancy Farm picnic, which is a political tradition in Kentucky. An accompanying statement from the office of the attending physician of Congress said Mr. McConnell “has maintained a strenuous course of physical therapy and rehabilitation,” and that his bout with polio as child “continues to be a significant factor in his mobility.” There was another photograph showing Mr. McConnell, leaning on a pillow, and Ms. Chao.

Mr. Beshear said that was not enough.

“Even the attending physician’s written statement does not discuss your actual condition, including whether you can speak, reason or carry out your duties as a senator,” Mr. Beshear wrote.

Mr. Beshear’s punchy letter comes in contrast with the more muted approach taken by Mr. McConnell’s colleagues on Capitol Hill, where Senate Democrats have been cautious about discussing the former leader’s health. There is a long tradition on Capitol Hill of politely ignoring the obvious decline of aging or otherwise incapacitated lawmakers, although that has begun to change.

Former Senator Dianne Feinstein, Democrat of California, resisted calls to resign despite growing awareness that she faced memory and cognitive issues, and despite a two-month absence in 2023 while recovering from shingles. Ms. Feinstein died in office at the age of 90.

item.title: St. Paul Police Chief Filed Harassment Complaint Against the Mayor
item.description:
The police chief in St. Paul, Minn., has filed a sexual harassment complaint against the city’s mayor asserting that she behaved inappropriately toward him and other members of the police force during her first months on the job.

Chief Axel Henry, who has led the St. Paul Police Department since 2022, told top city officials in March about a series of incidents involving Mayor Kaohly Her, according to records reviewed by The Times. The records provide few details of the incidents.

The city has hired an outside law firm to conduct an investigation into the mayor’s conduct, the records show.

Mayor Her, who became the first woman to serve as St. Paul’s mayor when she took office in January, declined a request for an interview.

Matt Wagenius, a spokesman for the mayor, said in an emailed statement, that he could not answer questions about an ongoing investigation. “The mayor has deep respect for city employees and regrets any unintended impact her actions may have had,” he said.

Chief Henry also declined a request for an interview.

“Chief Henry will do everything to ensure that appropriate conduct is modeled and followed in the St. Paul Police Department,” Chris Madel, a lawyer representing the police chief, said.

It was uncertain how the investigation, which had not previously been disclosed publicly, was affecting business at City Hall. The inquiry was unfolding as St. Paul, a focus of a federal immigration crackdown earlier in the year, faces significant challenges, including a projected $26 million deficit as well as highly debated efforts to clear a large homeless encampment.

In an April 1 letter, Mr. Madel notified Irene Kao, the city attorney for St. Paul, that Chief Henry planned “to step forward as a formal complainant against the mayor after becoming aware that the mayor’s conduct has extended beyond isolated incidents and has included sexual harassment of subordinate city employees, including members of the Saint Paul Police Department.”

The independent review is being conducted by Cally Kjellberg-Nelson, an employment law expert at the law firm Resolute Law, according to records obtained by The Times. Ms. Kjellberg-Nelson did not immediately respond to an email seeking information about the status of her inquiry.

Mr. Wagenius said he did not know when the review would be completed. Asked whether its findings would be shared with the public, he added: “We will honor all applicable laws when making the determination on the report.”

Mr. Madel’s letter included a screenshot of a text message, which Mr. Madel said the mayor had sent to a city employee. It included an image, along with a message that read, “When she wraps you up in her blanket after you gave her a good weinering,” followed by two crying laughter emojis.

Chief Henry, a St. Paul native who rose through the ranks since joining the department in 1998, has kept a relatively low profile since former Mayor Melvin Carter appointed him to lead the department in November 2022 for a six-year term.

During his tenure, St. Paul has seen a drop in violent crime, which Chief Henry has attributed in part to an initiative to aggressively investigate nonfatal shootings.

At times, the department has faced criticism. Last year, City Council members and residents objected after officers used chemical irritants and projectiles against protesters during an immigration arrest.

Ms. Her, the daughter of Hmong refugees from Laos, spent part of her childhood in a refugee camp before moving to the United States in the 1970s.

She represented a St. Paul district in the Minnesota House of Representatives from 2019 to 2025. A moderate Democrat who worked in finance and nonprofits earlier in her career, Ms. Her served as policy director for the city of St. Paul during Mr. Carter’s first mayoral term.

She surprised the city’s political establishment by launching a run for mayor last August, leaving her only three months to campaign against her former ally, Mr. Carter, who was well established. She made history as the city’s first female mayor and as the first Asian person elected to the role.

Ms. Her campaigned aggressively and found broad support for her message that the city’s problems required a more assertive, responsive and business-savvy leader. She promised to revitalize the downtown district, make it easier for businesses to thrive, lower housing costs and to redouble efforts to protect undocumented residents from the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

Alain Delaquérière contributed research.

item.title: Domestic Abuse Allegations Rock an Ohio House Race
item.description:
A sordid, yearslong family drama involving two powerful Republican members of Congress from Ohio and allegations of domestic abuse is threatening to put a fairly safe G.O.P. House seat at risk in an already challenging midterm election year for the party.

Representative Max Miller, a second-term Republican representing northeast Ohio whose political rise was fueled by his close relationship to President Trump, has been accused by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, of domestic abuse against her and their 2-year-old daughter.

Ms. Moreno, the daughter of Senator Bernie Moreno, also an Ohio Republican, has said that Mr. Miller scalded her chest and stomach by throwing hot water from a skillet at her body; held a gun to her head; pushed her against a wall and hit her head; and fractured their daughter’s collarbone and bruising her shoulder.

According to court documents, their daughter at one point told Ms. Moreno, “Daddy kill you.”

Mr. Miller has not only denied it all, he has gone on offense against Ms. Moreno, making damaging accusations of his own in a series of media interviews, court filings and countersuits that have kept the family’s personal trauma in the headlines. He has called his ex-wife mentally ill, a liar, a stalker and a dangerous individual who has made him and their daughter unsafe.

The legal and public relations war has in recent weeks risen to the level of a serious concern to Mr. Trump’s political operation, as well as White House officials, who are keenly aware that every seat matters as they stare down an electoral map that shows them at risk of losing their House majority.

They worry that Mr. Miller is harming his re-election chances and Republicans’ hopes of preserving the seat, according to three people familiar with internal discussions who spoke about them on the condition of anonymity.

And Democrats, who initially had little hope of flipping the seat, are newly bullish about their chances in the district, tempered only by a worry that Republicans may intervene and replace Mr. Miller on the ballot before an Aug. 5 deadline.

Mr. Miller, however, angrily disputed the notion that his seat was in jeopardy in a series of text messages in which he threatened to block a reporter’s number for seeking comment about the matter.

“Texas is turning blue like I’m losing my seat,” he wrote in one text. “Take a hike. After I win by more than my district, don’t bother ever contacting me again.” Mr. Miller added: “You’re disgusting,” noting that his child was involved, and saying that any such story was “trash.”

He has continued to rage at Ms. Moreno publicly.

In a recent interview with Spectrum News, Mr. Miller said that his ex-wife “sadly isn’t all there.”

In court, he has accused Ms. Moreno of making “repeated false reports” to child protective services, medical professionals, law enforcement and others. He has filed a defamation lawsuit against Ms. Moreno, saying she was running a smear campaign against him.

He has claimed that Ms. Moreno has untreated bipolar disorder, and said she is stalking him and trying to damage his reputation. He has told the court that he fears for his safety because of Ms. Moreno’s “vindictive and unpredictable behavior,” asserting that she owns at least one handgun, and claimed that their daughter’s collarbone injury was caused by Ms. Moreno’s reckless driving.

Ms. Moreno’s lawyer, Andrew Zashin, has said that she does not own a handgun, and Mr. Miller has not specified what kind or where it is. Her lawyer has also said she does not have a diagnosis of bipolar disorder. (Mr. Miller has sued Mr. Zashin.)

The recent conduct of Mr. Miller, who was once close with the president as well as Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, has become a source of frustration in the president’s circle, according to people familiar with their thinking. Many of them view his political problems as ones of his own making, and his to fix.

According to internal polling research by Democrats, Mr. Miller appears just one percentage point ahead of his Democratic challenger, Brian Poindexter, in a district that Mr. Trump won by double digits in 2024. The Democratic campaign arm has yet to spend any money in the district highlighting the claims against Mr. Miller, which aides said they planned to do.

“If all the allegations prove to be true,” Mr. Poindexter said in an interview, “Miller should be in jail, not worried about retaining a seat in Congress.”

Republicans close to Mr. Trump said they had viewed private polling that was also alarming for Mr. Miller’s candidacy. A spokeswoman for the party’s House campaign arm did not respond to a request for comment on the race.

A spokeswoman for Mr. Miller’s campaign, Abigail Angelos, noted that the court has continued to permit Mr. Miller joint custody of his child, undermining the credibility of what she called “outrageous accusations” against him. She said Mr. Miller would “continue to vigorously defend his reputation against false and reckless allegations designed to inflame public opinion rather than reflect reality.”

Mr. Miller is not the only House Republican facing allegations and investigations that could complicate their re-election efforts. In Florida, Representative Cory Mills was investigated by the Metropolitan Police Department in Washington last year in connection with a report of an assault on a woman. His former girlfriend was issued a protective order against him after accusing him of threatening her with revenge porn after their breakup. He has also been under investigation by the House Ethics Committee, and has vehemently denied wrongdoing.

And Representative Chuck Edwards of North Carolina is under investigation by the House Ethics Committee for allegations of sexual harassment in his office. Mr. Edwards has denied those allegations.

But Mr. Miller’s case is, perhaps, the most shocking and detailed, and involves a family drama that has ripped apart the G.O.P. delegation representing Ohio and pitted two MAGA loyalists against each other.

Mr. Moreno has remained publicly quiet about the case, which has created an awkward disconnect between both men’s political interest — keeping Mr. Miller’s seat in Republican hands — and the family feud.

A spokeswoman for Mr. Moreno, Reagan McCarthy, said that “Senator Moreno’s top priority is the safety and well-being of his daughter and granddaughter.” The spokeswoman added: “While he will not litigate these matters in the media or respond to baseless public attacks, he will do whatever it takes to ensure a just outcome for his family.”

Mr. Miller and Ms. Moreno first met while working on Marco Rubio’s presidential campaign in 2015, but rekindled their relationship years later, after Mr. Miller’s star took off when he joined the White House as director of Mr. Trump’s advance team and became close with the president.

During the first Trump term, Mr. Miller was known internally at the White House as “The Music Man,” for his role in queuing up the president’s favorite show tunes, including “Memory” from “Cats,” when he was in a foul mood.

He was the president’s loyal choice to challenge Representative Anthony Gonzalez, one of 10 House Republicans who voted to impeach him after the Jan. 6, 2021, mob attack on the Capitol.

“Max — great guy, I can tell you,” the president said at a 2021 rally in Ohio. “He’s a great guy.”

Mr. Gonzalez promptly retired instead of seeking re-election.

Ms. Moreno left campaign politics behind to create a dating app for Trump supporters. She and Mr. Miller were married at Mr. Trump’s Bedminster golf club in 2022, with Mr. Trump and close allies including Richard Grenell and Kellyanne Conway in attendance.

For a moment in time, the union looked like it would be a boon for Mr. Miller’s career. His new father-in-law, a wealthy former car dealer and hard-right Republican, donated tens of thousands of dollars to his various campaign committees. Mr. Moreno was elected to the Senate in 2024, after defeating Senator Sherrod Brown, Democrat of Ohio.

But the golden era was short-lived. The couple filed for divorce almost two years to the day after the wedding and have been stuck in a cycle of competing lawsuits revealing details of their personal lives ever since.

Ms. Moreno is not the first woman to level domestic abuse allegations against Mr. Miller. In her memoir, Stephanie Grisham, the former White House press secretary, wrote that she dated someone else in the administration who was physically abusive; she later acknowledged she had referred to Mr. Miller.

Mr. Miller denied her allegations and sued her for defamation, claiming she was trying to ruin his campaign for Congress.

But in his recent media tour, he has also managed to reopen his years-old court battle with Ms. Grisham. Earlier this month, Ms. Grisham sued Mr. Miller, claiming he broke their nondisclosure agreement, part of a 2023 settlement, in an interview and in a social media post in which he claims she fabricated the abuse.

item.title: Ghost Gun Was Used in Seattle Festival Shooting, Police Say
item.description:
Seattle police said Tuesday that the 15-year-old arrested on Sunday after a shooting at a food festival that left three dead and at least four wounded, including a toddler, had used a ghost gun, an untraceable firearm assembled without serial numbers.

The youth apprehended in the closing hours of a food festival near the city’s Space Needle had used a weapon that included an extended 33-round magazine, Seattle Police Chief Shon Barnes said. Nineteen rounds remained when he was brought into custody. The gun was created using parts from Polymer80, a now-shuttered manufacturer of weapons kits.

“For those who may be unfamiliar, a ghost gun is an untraceable weapon that lacks a serial number,” Mr. Barnes said. “They are typically homemade, and they are illegal.”

Last year, the Supreme Court upheld federal restrictions imposed on ghost guns by the Biden administration. The regulations required some level of traceability on the parts used to make the weapons, as well as background checks on the buyers of those parts.

Those restrictions have been challenged by the national gun lobby and conservative legal groups, and the popularity of the weapons has continue to rise, particularly among convicted felons, minors and others barred from buying firearms.

While they have been linked to mass shootings in the past, such as a 2019 school shooting in California, gun-safety groups say ghost guns are most frequently used in day-to-day street violence. Seattle’s assistant police chief, Nicole Powell, said Monday that investigators believe the Seattle Center shooting was gang-related, with two groups exchanging fire.

In 2019 and 2022, Washington State passed laws to combat untraceable firearms that are considered among the nation’s most comprehensive. But the weapons remain a growing problem. In January, a 26-year-old Seattle man was sentenced to prison after police raided his apartment in 2024, finding a 3-D printer and dozens of firearms, including 20 homemade guns.

Nationally, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives said the number of ghost guns recovered by law enforcement in 2022 and 2023 grew 44 percent compared to the preceding five years, and rose by nearly 1,600 percent between 2017 to 2023.

One suspected shooter in Sunday’s attack, Junior Cee Niko Semo, was among the three killed, police say. They are continuing to search for a third suspect.
